abstract: We develop a novel correlation forecasting model and integrate it with nonlinear shrinkage techniques to enhance the predictive performance of high-dimensional integrated covariance matrices (ICM). Within this framework, adapting the HARQ specification to the correlation domain allows our model to dynamically respond to measurement errors. Furthermore, we calibrate the unconditional correlation matrix via nonlinear shrinkage to mitigate spectral bias and employ noise-robust estimators (QMLE/PAV) to improve volatility forecasts. Extensive simulations and empirical portfolio analyses demonstrate that this approach reduces covariance forecasting errors and achieves high Sharpe ratios, including after transaction costs.
title: A HARQ-based framework for forecasting large covariance matrices using high-frequency data

abstract: Green finance policies have become important instruments for promoting renewable energy investment, yet their interaction with energy taxes remains insufficiently examined. Using panel data from 30 OECD countries over the period 2000–2023, this study analyzes the combined effects of green finance and energy taxation through panel regression and moderation models. The results yield four main findings. First, green finance policies significantly promote renewable energy investment, and the result remains robust across alternative specifications. Second, energy taxes negatively moderate this relationship, indicating that a higher energy-tax revenue share may weaken the marginal effect of green finance policies. Third, the subgroup estimates reveal context-dependent effects across economic, external-support, technological, and sectoral conditions, with formal tests providing additional support for several of these dimensions. Fourth, the subgroup estimates suggest that the interaction between green finance and energy taxation is positive in high-ODA contexts but negative in mature economies, medium-ODA contexts, countries with weaker environmental technology, and economies with high service-sector energy consumption. These findings highlight the need for context-specific policy coordination to avoid potential crowding-out between green finance and energy taxation.
title: Green finance policies, energy taxation, and renewable energy investment: Evidence from OECD countries

abstract: We use detailed, individual-level, panel data to relate growing political polarization to (i) changing beliefs about the pace of global warming and (ii) the propensity to make climate-friendly investment decisions. Individuals in our study were exogenously exposed to forest fires to varying degrees in the summer of 2018. While exposure increased the perceived pace of climate change on average, the response is attenuated in areas experiencing increases in right-wing populism, especially when local environmental media coverage was stronger. Changing beliefs also predict climate-friendly investment, but this is heavily mediated by the same political dynamics.
title: Populism, polarization and green investment

abstract: This study analyzes how spatial resolution and cross-sectoral interactions shape future modeled outcomes for the United States energy system, using the Global Change Analysis Model (GCAM). The analysis of spatial resolution considers two configurations: one representing the United States as a single region and another distinguishing each state as a separate region, using harmonized assumptions for all shared technologies. We find consistent high-level results, but demonstrate how the national resolution can be more accommodating to deployment of selected technologies where the use of nationally aggregated supply curves can mask geographic mismatches between low-cost production and demand. This is illustrated with hydrogen produced by renewable electrolysis, where low-cost production sites (e.g., the Northern Great Plains) are often quite far from major population and industrial centers. Cross-sectoral impacts from accelerated technological advances are weakest for buildings, greater for transportation, and strongest for electricity generation. In buildings, advanced technologies tend to increase electricity demand while also improving its efficiency. In contrast, improvements in the electricity generation sector drive nearly 400 TWh per year of additional electricity demand, primarily in industry and transportation, highlighting comparatively strong sectoral responses here. The study provides commentary on the implications of these results for the roles of single-sector as opposed to energy-system-wide modeling and analysis.
title: State or nation, sector or system? How granularity shapes U.S. energy modeling results

abstract: The electricity system in Great Britain (GB) allows participants to deliberately produce or consume a different volume to their traded position and has incentivised this practice with a single imbalance price since 2015. In particular, non-physical traders (NPTs) often take an open position to imbalance without any intention to produce or consume power. However, new government proposals could restrict this practice due to concerns over supply–demand balancing feasibility and costs. This article presents the first empirical analysis of speculative imbalance positioning (SIP) by NPTs in the GB electricity system through its effects on imbalance volumes, balancing costs, the imbalance price, and associated settlement costs over the period 2021–2024. Our research uses party-level imbalance data in each settlement period to run counterfactual simulations of the electricity balancing mechanism without the aggregate NPT imbalance. Our results indicate that SIP by NPTs reduced the total net balancing volume required by 3.1–3.9 TWh (16%–20%), reduced system imbalance standard deviation by 48–65 MWh (13%–17%), reduced balancing costs by £347–396m (5.9%–6.7%), and reduced supplier imbalance costs by £193–325m (65%–75%) over the analysis period. These results suggest that consumer bills would have been higher without SIP by NPTs, since the extra costs would likely have been passed on to consumers through levies, although the potential for effects in the wholesale (primarily late-stage intraday) markets complicates this picture.
title: Speculative imbalance positions by non-physical traders: Impacts on electricity system balancing in Great Britain

abstract: Immigrant women marry younger, have more children and exhibit worse labor market outcomes than native-born women in most industrial countries – partly due to persistent barriers to integration and the lack of targeted integration measures. We examine how improved degree recognition - an integration measure proven to enhance labor market outcomes - affects family formation and fertility among foreign-born women. To establish causality, we exploit the Federal Recognition Act that was implemented in 2012 in Germany within a flexible difference-in-difference framework. We find that post-reform, women from outside the European Union eligible to apply for standardized and facilitated degree recognition exhibit lower marriage rates, in particular their rates of intramarriage decrease. We also find significant effects on the quantum and timing of immigrant fertility, with evidence of convergence toward the fertility patterns of native-born women. A large fraction of these effects can be attributed to improved labor market outcomes post-reform. Our findings, which prove robust to a number of identification and robustness checks, underscore that integration measures that target the labor market can have crucial implications for family formation and fertility decisions of foreign-born women with previously low labor market attachment.
title: Degrees of disruption: The impact of professional degree recognition on family formation and fertility of migrant women

abstract: Brandt et al. (2025) prove an impossibility result for budget aggregation under ℓ1 and ℓ∞ preferences, and leave the intermediate ℓ p preferences with 1 < p < ∞ as an open question. We further study this problem for budget aggregation under strictly convex norm-induced preferences, which include all intermediate ℓ p preferences. Our main result shows that, with at least three projects and at least two voters, no budget aggregation mechanism satisfies strategy-proofness, Pareto efficiency, and sign proportionality. In particular, it applies to all ℓ p preferences with 1 < p < ∞. It therefore settles, for the intermediate ℓ p norms, the conjecture posed by Brandt et al. (2025), and strengthens the conjectured weak fairness property from proportionality to sign proportionality. Sign proportionality is a relaxation of proportionality. It only requires that every project with positive support receives a positive division.
title: Strategy-proofness, Pareto efficiency, and sign proportionality in budget aggregation with strictly convex norm-induced preferences: An impossibility result

abstract: Geopolitical risk predicts a deterioration in U.S. investment-at-risk. A 30-point increase in historical GPR is associated with a 1.8-percentage-point decline in the fifth conditional percentile of next-quarter investment growth,compared with 0.15 percentage points at the mean. Median and upper-tail estimates are close to zero. The pattern survives financial and macroeconomic controls. Monthly time-varying local projections identify responses under the restriction that other economic shocks do not affect GPR within the month. Identified shocks persistently lower the fifth percentile relative to the median, with larger responses during high-GPR episodes.
title: Geopolitical risk and U.S. investment-at-risk

abstract: Energy communities are becoming an important instrument of the clean energy transition, but their performance depends on how they are governed. We develop a model in which a municipality invests in renewable-energy infrastructure and chooses between public management and delegation to a private aggregator. Consumers differ in their willingness to pay, value self-produced energy, and incur privacy costs when consumption data are used beyond the operational baseline. Under the symmetric benchmark, private governance produces a smaller community because the aggregator applies a monopoly participation margin and does not internalize the benefit that additional members create for the rest of the community. Public governance therefore expands participation, while investment timing depends on how the operating surplus is allocated between the municipality, members, and the private operator. We then show that correcting the private participation distortion is only a partial alignment result: implementing the public-optimal community size does not by itself align member utility or investment timing. A regulated delegation contract can use a per-member inclusion payment to align participation, a membership-independent concession payment to align investment timing, and data-use restrictions to control privacy exposure. Finally, a numerical example relaxes operational symmetry by allowing the private operator to manage self-consumption more efficiently than the public operator. In this case, regulated delegation can combine public participation objectives with private operational efficiency when the relevant contractual margins are observable and enforceable.
title: Who should govern public energy communities? The role of environmental awareness and privacy cost

abstract: Recent Sustainable Development Goals focus on reducing poverty. Poverty alleviation programs (PAPs) are now a key part of social policy as they provide sustained support to vulnerable populations, helping lift them out of poverty and break the cycle of intergenerational poverty, contributing to a more stable and cohesive society. This paper presents an adverse selection model with two types of agents (Rich and Poor), where the government aims to minimize the cost of a Poverty Alleviation Program while ensuring that everyone has access to a minimum income. By considering differences in income-generating ability or disutility of labor, we study the effectiveness of workfare and monitoring as tools to prevent fraud in the PAP. When income generating ability is unknown, the optimal PAP depends on the proportion of Rich agents, monitoring costs, and the productivity gap between the two types. When agents differ in their disutility of labor, the optimal PAP does not include workfare. We also consider the choice of the policy objective by comparing a minimum income target with a minimum utility target, following the perspective emphasized by Wane (2001). Under quasi-linear preferences, the main mechanisms underlying the use of monitoring and workfare continue to apply, and most results remain unchanged. However, when agents differ in their income generating ability and workfare exceeds the privately optimal labour supply, a minimum utility objective makes workfare more costly (and monitoring too, if both are used).
title: Combating fraud in poverty alleviation programs: should we use monitoring, workfare or both?

abstract: Many economic studies have identified barriers to migration which can distort labor allocation and productivity, but comparing the macroeconomic importance of each barrier is complicated by variation in study design and sampling. We build and estimate a dynamic general-equilibrium model of rural–urban migration which nests several of the key frictions emphasized in the literature. We discipline the model using large-scale data from Kenya—the site of several recent migration experiments—and simulate each experiment within the model. We proceed to estimate the long-run treatment effects of each intervention, the macroeconomic effects of scaling interventions to the national level, and the aggregate importance of each migration friction. Our findings shed light on the lack of a migration response to large unconditional cash transfers, and reveal how treatment impacts on migration can rise over time as the constraints relaxed by an intervention interact with subsequent productivity shocks.
title: The macroeconomic effects of lifting barriers to migration

abstract: Punishment is a well-established mechanism for sustaining cooperation in public goods games. The standard Post-Punishment rule, in which punishment decisions are made after observing others’ contributions, may operate at least partly through “hot” emotion-driven responses to norm violations. This paper develops and experimentally tests a novel Pre-Punishment rule, in which subjects commit to a contribution threshold before observing others’ contributions, and group members who fall below this threshold are punished automatically. Unlike the Post-Punishment rule, punishment under the Pre-Punishment rule is not targeted toward identified free riders but instead operates as an impersonal, rule-based enforcement mechanism. Combining behavioral data with biometric measures of emotional arousal, we find that the two rules are equally effective in sustaining cooperation. However, they operate through different psychological channels. Under the Post-Punishment rule, emotional arousal in response to observing free riding predicts the subsequent punishment decisions, whereas this relationship is absent under the Pre-Punishment rule. Moreover, punished subjects exhibit greater emotional arousal, but this emotional response does not translate into larger subsequent contributions under either rule. These findings highlight the possibility of designing “cool” rule-based enforcement mechanisms that retain the cooperative benefits of punishment while reducing its emotional and interpersonal costs.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
source_issue: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 253
title: “Hot” and “Cold” punishment in public goods provision

abstract: By focusing on gender differences, this study examines the impact of teleworkability on labour market outcomes amid the COVID-19 pandemic in South Korea. Using a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) framework, we ascertain that teleworkability mitigated employment shocks during the pandemic, primarily by reducing transitions into furlough or unemployment, which consequently mitigated declines in wages and working hours. Moreover, teleworkability’s protective effect was more pronounced for women, who experienced greater labour market shocks. These gender differences stem from a stronger protective effect in the social and non-essential sectors, where women are more heavily represented. In contrast to previous studies, we find no significant differences in teleworkability’s impact based on childcare responsibilities. Our findings highlight teleworkability’s role in enhancing labour market resilience and provide policy insights for pandemic preparedness and gender-sensitive labour market policies.
title: Teleworkability and labour market resilience during COVID-19: gender differences in South Korea

abstract: The surge in energy demand brought about by the development of artificial intelligence (AI) not only intensifies global energy consumption pressures but also poses challenges to environmental sustainability. Using panel data from 281 Chinese cities during 2015–2022 and leveraging the establishment of next-generation AI innovation pilot zones as a quasi-natural experiment, we investigate how AI pilot zones influence the rebound effect of electricity consumption. Our analysis reveals that AI pilot zones significantly amplify the urban electricity consumption rebound, especially in cities with high coal dependency, low digital economy levels, and lower total factor productivity. Mechanism analysis indicates that AI policies enhance energy utilization efficiency and promote industrial upgrading, reinforcing the rebound effect. Further, environmental regulation, particularly penalties, can mitigate this impact. These findings deepen understanding of the Jevons paradox in the AI context and offer empirical evidence for balancing AI-driven energy transformation with low-carbon development.

title: Artificial intelligence policies and the rebound effect of electricity consumption: Evidence from China

abstract: Job postings serve as one of the primary means to communicate with prospective employees, enabling employers to highlight the benefits of the position and attract qualified applicants. As work-from-home flexibility has become increasingly prevalent, this study examines whether employers strategically disclose work-from-home flexibility in their job postings and how this disclosure is associated with hiring outcomes. Using a comprehensive sample of job postings from US employers between 2017 and 2024, we find that employers are more likely to disclose work-from-home flexibility when facing greater labor market competition and that disclosing this flexibility is associated with a higher job vacancy filling rate, especially when work-from-home information is disclosed in a more salient manner. However, we document a positive association between work-from-home disclosures and subsequent employee turnover, suggesting potential costs associated with these disclosures. These findings add to the growing literature on firms’ strategic disclosure targeted towards labor markets.
title: Disclosing work-from-home flexibility to compete for talent? Evidence from job postings

abstract: Motivated by the spread of crises in the euro area, we propose an open-economy New Keynesian model of a monetary union, highlighting two features of the financial market: cross-border sovereign bond holdings and financial heterogeneity. Cross-border bond holdings, together with financial heterogeneity, propagate sovereign-risk shocks throughout the monetary union. While core economies are more resilient to shocks due to lower risks associated with sovereign bonds and financial intermediaries, cross-border bond holdings create a shock transmission channel from the periphery to the core. Consequently, the core bears a larger share of the impact than it otherwise would, while the periphery faces a more contained peak impact than under financial autarky. Considering the two financial-market features we highlight and the limitations of the unified interest-rate policy, unconventional tools (e.g., QE and macroprudential policy) prove effective in dealing with sovereign-risk shocks by directly targeting sovereign bonds and financial intermediaries’ balance sheets.
title: Cross-border sovereign bond holdings and unconventional policies in a monetary union

abstract: We consider the fair allocation of indivisible goods with binary valuations. In this setting, the maximum Nash welfare rule, the leximin rule, and all additive welfarist rules with a strictly concave function coincide. We show that for any number of agents, this rule is the only rule that satisfies envy-freeness up to one good, strategyproofness, neutrality, minimal completeness, and invariance under disapproving unassigned goods (IDU). Moreover, we present an alternative characterization for two agents, where we replace IDU with non-redundancy and resource-monotonicity. In both characterizations, all axioms are necessary.
title: Fair division with binary valuations: Characterizations

abstract: China, the EU, and the US are all expanding their export controls on items with both civilian and military applications. This column combines data on US exports with a quantitative trade model to examine the effects of export controls on dual-use goods. When the US and its allies impose controls together, target countries’ imports of controlled goods fall 5.7 times as much as under unilateral US controls. Coordination delivers a larger security gain for the US, measured as the rise in US real military spending relative to target countries, at a similar cost to civilians in terms of incomes and prices of goods.
authors: Jingting Fan, Kyle Handley, Nuno Limão

title: Export controls are broader than you think, but they buy more security with coordination

abstract: Rising housing costs have intensified affordability crises across Europe. This column examines the drivers of this growth, its distributional effects on households, and implications for labour mobility. While the pre-global financial crisis rise in house prices was largely driven by credit supply, housing supply constraints have become a more important driver of prices in recent years. Housing affordability pressures are highly uneven across location, housing tenure, income groups, and the level of urbanisation, and have widened income and wealth gaps between owners and renters. Beyond distributional concerns, declining affordability also has adverse consequences for labour allocation and efficiency.
authors: Robert Beyer, Nina Biljanovska, Alexandra Fotiou, Morgan Maneely, Frederik Toscani

title: Locked out: Drivers and consequences of housing affordability pressures in Europe

abstract: Improving the effectiveness of residential energy-saving interventions is an important policy issue in demand-side management, yet such interventions are often constrained by the attitude-behavior gap and the difficulty of sustaining behavioral change over time. In addition, evidence remains limited on how intervention effects vary with household demographic and psychological heterogeneities. Drawing on a 16-week field experiment involving 267 households in Singapore, this study evaluates a combined intervention based on goal setting and information framing by integrating hourly electricity-use records with a structured questionnaire of 88 items covering energy-saving behaviors, personality traits, thinking styles, values, and demographic characteristics. Using a difference-in-differences framework with two-way fixed effects, this study estimates both the average and heterogeneous effects of the combined intervention. The results show that the largest average reduction in residential energy consumption across the combined interventions was 5.3%. From the perspective of heterogeneity, high-income and highly educated households are particularly responsive to environmental framing, with energy-saving effects reaching 5.39% and 5.62%, respectively. In the 10% monetary group, a one-unit increase in conscientiousness was associated with an estimated increase in electricity savings of approximately 11.6 percentage points. These findings underscore the importance of targeted demand-side policies rather than uniform intervention strategies. Specifically, with the energy-saving goal held constant, environmental framing yielded larger estimated electricity savings than monetary framing among high-income and highly educated households. Conscientiousness, altruistic values, and a holistic locus of attention were associated with greater energy savings under monetary framing. Overall, this study provides policy-relevant evidence for designing targeted and cost-effective residential energy conservation policies.
title: Targeting residential energy conservation through combined goal setting and information framing: Evidence from a field experiment in Singapore

abstract: The number of Nash equilibria of the mixed extension of a generic finite game in normal form is finite and odd. This raises the question how large the number can be, depending on the number of players and the numbers of their pure strategies. Here we present a lower bound for the maximal possible number in the case of n -player games where each player has two pure strategies. It is surprisingly close to a known upper bound.
title: Maximal number of mixed Nash equilibria in generic games where each player has two pure strategies

abstract: The energy transition is driving profound employment restructuring, as emerging technologies have different labour requirements compared to conventional technologies. Previous studies have underestimated the associated inter-sectoral employment effects because of inadequate modelling of energy technologies and the absence of employment induced by household consumption. This research applies the Python for Power System Analysis China (PyPSA-China) framework at a provincial spatial resolution and hourly temporal resolution to identify optimised investments in energy technologies. A partially-closed, multi-regional input-output (PC-MRIO) model is then developed to quantify technology-specific employment effects, including direct, indirect, and household-consumption-induced effects. The study finds that early decarbonisation of China's power system can reduce employment loss resulting from stranded assets and better aligns with industrial upgrades. Under the early and steady decarbonisation pathway, employment associated with the modelled power system would reach approximately 11 million jobs by 2060, with household-consumption-induced employment contributing more than 34% of the total. However, decarbonisation also leads to regionally unequal labour reallocation across regions and demographic groups. The rising Gini coefficient, which assesses regional value-added distribution based on employment shares, indicates an increasing concentration of stable, high-value-added jobs in a few developed eastern coastal regions such as Jiangsu. Fossil-fuel-dependent regions with inadequate renewable energy industry foundations and limited household consumption affordability face heightened vulnerability; examples include Shanxi and Guizhou. Decarbonisation promotes middle-income expansion, but disadvantages certain groups, including females, middle-aged workers, and those with limited education. These findings highlight the need for targeted support for exposed regions and demographic groups.

title: Power system decarbonisation and unequal labour reallocation across regions and demographics in China

abstract: We document “climate extrapolation” by exploiting a unique feature of the wine market: global comparability and locally determined prices. Using a novel dataset of Bordeaux Premier Cru auctions, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in relative climate attention is associated with a 2.08% price decrease for identical bottles sold in the same month. This result aligns with the availability heuristic, as it is stronger during periods when the impact of climate change is more palpable. The discount is consistent with concerns from investors, who demand climate-risk premia for lower-quality wines, and from consumers, who exhibit an aversion to wines near the end of their optimal consumption window.
title: Climate extrapolation and relative asset prices: Evidence from Bordeaux Premier Cru wine auctions

abstract: Prediction contests may distort forecasts; can they identify expertise? A conventional contest consistently selects the expert minimizing expected posterior loss in every Bayesian Nash equilibrium. We assume a common prior, independent binary questions with finite signal supports, a finite report set containing every posterior belief, a fixed number of experts and a loss gap bounded away from zero. A truthful deviation wins with high probability against arbitrary rival strategies. When the best expert’s signal makes each rival’s information redundant, fewer questions suffice; a matching two-expert lower bound establishes the optimal order in the loss gap and error tolerance.
title: Can prediction contests select the best expert despite strategic reporting?

abstract: Since mid-1980s. convergence literature has proposed or examined empirically the following hypothesis: a) poorer countries’ incomes grow faster, b) their income level grows more than the income level of richer countries, c) resulting in convergence in income levels across countries. This paper emphasizes that faster growth in incomes, or β-convergence, does not imply a reduction in income differences. We define the convergence rate and directly test the convergence hypothesis. With data from three different sources (World Development Indicators, Maddison Project database, and Penn World Tables) from 1960 to 2024, we demonstrate unconditional and conditional divergence from the smallest (OECD) to the largest group of countries. Further, both in general and for the OECD, the lower the initial income greater is the divergence rate and this pattern is stronger for higher income countries. We show it is the divergence of TFP from the world technological frontier that explains divergence in incomes.
title: Divergence: Unconditional, Conditional and in OECD

abstract: We study a dynamic political economy model in which two ideologically opposed parties alternate in power and set a one-dimensional policy that becomes the next period’s status quo. Policy change is costly, with costs potentially distributed asymmetrically between the parties. Pareto-efficient policy paths are monotone, and constant policies are efficient if and only if moderate. We characterize stationary Markov perfect equilibria in cutoff strategies: parties correct extreme status quos and maintain moderate ones. Policy reversals arise only under high polarization, when the equilibrium is unique and features perpetual reversals. High adjustment costs do not ensure efficiency: an incumbent cost advantage induces preemptive overshooting, whereas an opposition advantage produces free-riding and inaction. When polarization and cost imbalance are both low, all steady-state equilibrium policies are efficient. With convex rather than linear adjustment costs, inertia takes the form of gradualism. From an extreme status quo under high or very low polarization, welfare is locally highest when costs are balanced; from a moderate status quo, higher costs can improve welfare by dampening policy fluctuations.
title: Efficiency with Political Power Dynamics and Costly Policy Change

abstract: Religious rituals often generate synchronized economic activity and large-scale movement of people and goods with important public health consequences. This paper studies the link between the Islamic festival of Eid al-Adha, which mandates ritual animal sacrifice, and livestock infections. Using a new country–product–month panel comprising sixty Muslim countries and three halal livestock categories from 2004 to 2019, we examine whether Eid related international trade exposure or domestic livestock circulation result in higher livestock infections. Results show that country–product pairs with greater historical exposure to live animal imports during Eid periods experience significantly larger increases in livestock infections around Eid. Health impacts dissipate rapidly, vanishing after two months. In contrast, estimates based on domestic mobility exposure are sensitive to alternative functional forms, regional composition, and road infrastructure measures, precluding robust inference about this channel. The findings document a previously underexplored channel through which large-scale religious rituals may influence animal health and disease transmission.
title: Religious rituals, livestock mobility and infectious diseases: Evidence from Eid al-Adha
